extracted.intended_audience: educated readers interested in cultural criticism, politics, and 19th-century social theory
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading / extraction of normative criteria and evaluative claims from Matthew Arnold's essay 'Culture and Anarchy', concerning culture, authority, classes, and the dangers of excessive individual liberty. The page is a literary-political essay offering standards for judging social institutions and qualities of classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central idea: assertion of personal liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The central idea of English life and politics is the assertion of personal liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold states this as a fundamental national idea and uses it as the starting point for critique: as feudal subordination dies out, the English notion that 'it is the great right and happiness of an Englishman to do as far as possible what he likes' risks drifting into disorder. This criterion is invoked to explain why other institutional checks (e.g., a strong conception of the State) are weak in England.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worship of freedom (doing as one likes) as source of anarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere devotion to the freedom to 'do as one likes' tends toward anarchy when unbalanced by ideas of public duty or right reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples Arnold adduces include mass assertions of liberty (marching, assembling, hooting, smashing), inflammatory lectures, and riots; he argues that such impulses, when culturally valorised, become less 'trifling' and more frequent, producing social disintegration unless countered by authority guided by light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture defined as pursuit of perfection and light
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture simply means trying to perfect oneself; it brings 'light' which shows that mere freedom is not the highest good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold defines culture as the disinterested pursuit of perfection through reading, observing, and thinking; culture supplies 'a principle of authority' (right reason) that can counteract tendencies to anarchy. He distinguishes this notion of culture from 'machinery' or instrumental reforms called 'culture' by some contemporaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority should rest on right reason (light) rather than on class interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The true seat of authority in society should be the State as the power representing the right reason of the nation; culture helps identify who is fit to wield it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold surveys aristocracy, middle-class, and working-class to test which could embody 'light'. He insists culture can judge 'qualifications and titles to our confidence' and thus render practical service in choosing authority, rather than entrusting rule to a class simply because of birth, wealth, or numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscription as a means to instil public duty and discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal military service (conscription) brings the idea of public duty and discipline to raw masses who otherwise lack it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold cites Michelet's remark that conscription civilised the French masses by teaching public duty; he contrasts this with English resistance to conscription (example from Clay Cross) to explain why English working classes lack the same sense of subordinate public duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy: virtues (dignity, politeness, serenity) and limitations (want of light)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocracies possess sweetness, dignity, politeness, serenity and high spirit but are often inaccessible to ideas and 'unapt to see how the world is going', making them inadequate in epochs of expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold argues aristocracies are valuable as foils (educative shadow) but, in times when ideas and change dominate, their attachment to established fact and lack of 'light' render them bewildered and ineffective. He uses examples (Lord Elcho as mean; Sir Thomas Bateson as excess) to illustrate balance and danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle-class: industrialism and liberal reforms as 'machinery' lacking inner light
rubrics_metrics.description: The middle-class has achieved reforms (free-trade, parliamentary reform, abolition of church-rates, voluntaryism) but often treats these as machinery without sufficient inner 'light' or pursuit of perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold critiques middle-class complacency and self-satisfaction (Mr. Bazley's famous complacent claim about middle-class education), arguing that the middle-class's achievements often appear instrumental and not evidence of culture. Representative figures (Jacob Bright, Bazley, Rev. W. Cattle) illustrate mean and excess and demonstrate the class's limits as a seat of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working-class: energy and honesty but lack of cultivated light
rubrics_metrics.description: The working-class has ready powers of action and honesty, but as yet is 'raw and uncultivated' and therefore lacks the light culture provides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold notes readiness to act (Hyde Park example), but that without culture the working-class's energy can be misdirected; he uses figures (Mr. Odger as mean, Mr. Bradlaugh as excess) to show the potential and perils of placing authority in the working-class prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation method: use of 'mean' and 'excess' (Aristotelian virtue ethics) to judge classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnold applies Aristotle's notion of virtue as a mean between excess and defect to assess classes: find representative men who embody each class's mean (virtue) and excess (vice) to judge suitability for authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He explicitly invokes Aristotle's machinery learned at Oxford and compares pairs (Lord Elcho / Sir Thomas Bateson; Jacob Bright / Rev. W. Cattle; Mr. Odger / Mr. Bradlaugh) to illustrate how to discern a class's strengths and dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law's formality and officials' reluctance to enforce it facilitates liberty-as-impulse
rubrics_metrics.description: Because English law is made with an eye to the English impulse to 'do as he likes' and lacks discretionary administrative power, individuals gain advantage and authorities may decline to enforce laws, reinforcing the assertion of personal liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold observes that laws were made for different circumstances and that their strict letter may favour the libertarian Englishman; enforcement can be avoided or laws abolished, and magistrates or military forces often do not act even when disorder occurs (examples: municipal and militia officers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between sentimental idea of country and practical idea of State
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people have the sentiment of 'country' but lack the conception of the State as a working power capable of exercising authority for the common good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold suggests this deficiency explains reluctance to accept State authority: Englishmen are accustomed to living within class identities and sentiments rather than a collective conception of the State that legitimately restrains individual liberty for common advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and conscientiousness can produce reluctance to wield coercive authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The honesty common to English classes leads to moral hesitation about using force or coercive power even when social disorder might require it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold gives the example of the Alderman-Colonel who refused to let militia intervene in street disorder for fear of bloodshed, interpreting this as a sign that middle-class honesty disqualifies it from the authoritative role it might otherwise be thought fit to assume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture's practical benefit: impartial judging and seeing the good in all
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture confers the ability to look at 'ins and outs' impartially, without hatred or partiality, and to see the good in everybody—thus enabling just selection and exercise of authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold emphasizes culture's method—reading, observing, thinking—and claims its disinterested pursuit of perfection is the basis for right reason, which can harmonise ideas and provide a usable principle of authority against anarchy.
